#103179. Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

📅 2026-08-26 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (2990 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Smashingmagazine ↗ Open Full Page

Rethinking Data Visualisation: A UX Approach To Dashboards That Actually Drives Decisions

📅 2026-08-26 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In organisations today, data has never been more available.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Meriem Benhabiles is a Designer specialising in User Experience, with over five years working in-house, agency-side, and independently. Her background in … More about Meriem ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In organisations today, data has never been more available. Dashboards and performance decks exist for almost every function — sales, product, marketing, operations — and the tools to build them have never been more accessible. And yet, in weekly standups and quarterly reviews, the same thing happens constantly: someone shares the numbers, the room nods, and the meeting ends without a decision or clear direction.

When that happens, the data usually takes the blame. The numbers weren’t granular enough, the dataset wasn’t complete, we need more information before we can act. But the data is almost never the problem. The reality is that nobody designed it to deliver insights. The chart was built from what was available, not from the question that needed answering. The audience was assumed rather than understood, and what should actually change as a result of seeing this data — that question — was never asked at all.

Data visualisation and UX are solving the same underlying problem: both are trying to move the right information to the right person in a way that changes something. The vocabulary is different, but the underlying challenge is identical, and the moment you start treating them as complementary disciplines is the moment dashboards stop being a passive collection of charts and start doing something functional.

For designers who work with data, analysts who present to non-technical audiences, and marketers who need their numbers to do more than sit in a slide, this read is for you.

In a recent development, in 1973, the statistician Francis Anscombe (PDF) published a paper that made a quiet but clarifying point. He constructed four datasets that are statistically identical: same mean, same variance, same correlation coefficient, and same regression line. Run the numbers on any of them, and they are identical. Plot them, and they could not be more different.

Anscombe’s lesson to statisticians was about diagnosis: visualisation reveals the operational truth that raw numbers conceal.

According to recent reports, but visualisation isn’t just diagnostic; it is also communicative. The form you choose is where understanding either emerges or gets lost in the noise. Does your audience walk away with numbers, or with a story they’ll quote and talk about?

It has been revealed that one of the most striking examples is Visual Capitalist’s History of Pandemics. Instead of burying the reader in a massive data table of casualty counts, it maps the death toll of major historical pandemics using a proportional bubble layout on a single timeline.

Recent findings suggest that before your brain reads a single number, your visual system grasps the sheer scale of the Black Death relative to everything else on the page. The right visualisation does not just plot the data but makes the story impossible to miss.

Edward Tufte codified a foundational principle for the craft with his data-ink ratio: every mark on a chart should serve the data, not decorate it. It remains a widely used framework in data visualisation, anchored in the assumption that clarity and visual hygiene are the goal.

It has been revealed that for a chart in isolation, that holds. But a chart is never read in isolation: it’s read by a person, in a specific context, under specific pressure. Strip a chart down to its cleanest form, and you might be removing the exact layer of context a decision-maker needs. Simplicity isn’t the goal in itself; appropriate complexity is.

Data is a message, and the right amount of signal depends entirely on who’s receiving it.

Which leads to the core principle of data UX: roughly 80% of the work that determines whether a dashboard succeeds happens before you ever draw a chart.

That dependency is the thread the rest of this piece pulls on.

It has been revealed that the high-leverage 80% almost never happens on screen. It happens upstream: before a tool is opened, before a dataset is pulled, before a single design choice is made. It comes down to three questions, and once they become habitual, they change what you notice, what you ask, and what you push back on at the outset of every project.

Most data-heavy projects start backward: teams pull whatever metrics their internal analytics tools already track and build visualisations around them, while the question the data was supposed to answer either gets assumed or never gets asked. This happens simply because we anchor on the data in front of us as the boundary of what’s possible.

Industry observers note that defining a goal first sounds obvious, but in practice, it rarely happens with the necessary clarity. “Show me how the product is performing” is not a goal; “Identify which features drive retention among users who signed up in Q1” is, as it includes three things the first doesn’t: a metric, a population, and an implied action. That specificity is what converts an open-ended exploration into a constrained, answerable design problem. Which one you start from determines everything that follows: what you include, what comparisons matter, and what you leave out entirely.

Starting with available data produces a dashboard that answers no particular question, because it was never built for one — every number is present, none of them pointed anywhere. Starting with the operational question does the reverse: every element on the screen earns its place, because each one is there to help answer it.

Industry observers note that for example, consider a UX team trying to fix a leaky checkout flow for an e-commerce website. A data-first approach pulls everything available, from clicks to scroll depth and device types, yielding a massive dashboard that leaves everyone asking, “Okay, but what do we actually change?” A context-first approach starts with a constraint: “At which step of the checkout do people drop off?” By filtering out 90% of the noise, the team builds a simple funnel chart, instantly spots a bottleneck on the payment screen, and knows exactly what to redesign.

Designing for an audience comes down to two things: accountability and familiarity.

Familiarity is about data literacy. Do they read charts instinctively, or does a complex visualisation create friction? Handing a dense, multi-layered dashboard to a Head of Sales and a senior analyst is like giving the same map to someone who navigates by landmarks and someone who reads grid coordinates. The data is accurate, but it is only functional for one of them.

Sources indicate that accountability dictates how that complexity must be presented. A chart showing a 12% decline carries vastly different weight for the executive responsible for that number versus the analyst simply reporting it. Understanding your audience means grasping this relationship; data is never processed neutrally when your performance is on the line.

Together, familiarity and accountability decide one practical thing: how much you can put in front of someone.

In data visualisation, simplicity is not a fixed virtue — the right level of it is contingent on who is reading, and what they need to do.

Recent findings suggest that an analyst relies on a high-density environment to conduct diagnostic discovery. By isolating individual behaviour nodes and mapping out raw user flows, they interrogate the data at its atomic level to uncover the hidden insights and underperforming spend that will shape future campaigns.

An executive, by contrast, requires a highly synthesised translation of that data to immediately identify what is driving commercial growth. Tailoring a dashboard to your audience means adjusting the density dial, delivering maximum signal with appropriate complexity for the specific brain in the room.

Most data projects operate on the comfortable assumption that if a chart is accurate and clear, the insight will take care of itself. In reality, information and insight are entirely different states. Information is what the data shows, whereas insight is the specific decision, shift in understanding, or course correction someone makes as a result of seeing it. If the intended business change isn’t defined before the design begins, a dashboard will default to passive reporting rather than driving action.

Marketing and engineering teams experience the danger of this gap whenever a core business metric suddenly plummets.

According to recent reports, A dashboard built for information simply sounds the alarm, showing a chart that tracks a sharp 15% drop in booking rates. Because the data lacks depth, leadership defaults to panic: they immediately call the UX design team, assuming the app is broken or the checkout flow is flawed. Because the data doesn’t pinpoint the core of the problem, it triggers a costly, misplaced fire drill.

According to recent reports, A dashboard built for insight isolates the variables required to make an informed decision. Instead of a single, flat booking metric, the visualisation maps the drop against traffic sources and campaign rolls out — instantly revealing that while app performance and core user conversion are perfectly stable, the sitewide rate was artificially diluted by a massive influx of low-intent click traffic from a newly scaled campaign. The team doesn’t waste time redesigning a functioning app; they get the exact insight needed to pause the underperforming marketing campaign and adjust their acquisition strategy.

Every visualisation implies a next step, even if that step is “nothing needs to change right now.” The question is whether the design makes that implication clear enough for the viewer to recognise it.

According to recent reports, my aha moment in data visualisation happened during a project for a client-facing B2B SaaS platform focused on enterprise talent management and competency tracking in Pegasystems skills. The platform captured a massive footprint of daily telemetry, and the brief arrived open-ended: “We have an immense archive of user activity, now we need to present it to enterprise teams.”.

Industry observers note that we could very easily have charted everything that was captured, but we wouldn’t be doing end people any favours if they just ended up looking at a data graveyard. My responsibility immediately moved beyond pure interface craftsmanship; it became about architecting a highly practical tool for real people who would open this dashboard routinely and need it to tell them an honest, immediate story about their workflows.

Here is how the project actually went.

Recent findings suggest that the client believed this massive pool of data could help their people perform better, and wanted an interface that finally enabled that growth. Translating that broad ambition into tangible visualisations required defining the practical mechanics of performance. What variables indicate advancement vs passive usage? What does “perform better” actually mean? How do you measure it?

An obvious candidate was time spent by product. Every platform tracks it. It is easy to show, and it feels meaningful. But time spent is a proxy; it tells you someone was there, not whether they got anything out of it.

The more meaningful signals were competency scores by area, certification completion rates, and historical performance trajectories. Integrating time-spent data alongside these performance metrics added a useful layer of interpretation, helping us surface which modules consumers were underutilising and whether that directly correlated with lagging scores. Time spent became a supporting signal in the larger story.

The second question was about the appropriate level of granularity. An identical metric carries completely different weight depending on who is looking at it. An individual contributor tracking their own completion rate needs to know if they are pacing correctly, whereas a manager reviewing a team aggregate needs to know precisely who requires immediate support. This distinction shaped every subsequent data-exposure and filtering decision. Defining that structural story early determined exactly what to show, and to whom.

According to recent reports, the most straightforward approach to this design would have been predictable: use the same charts, but offer an individual view and an aggregated team view. Far too many dashboards rely on this shortcut, subtly tweaking the scale of identical data visualisations and labelling it “personalisation.”.

An authentic analysis of the audience reveals a much deeper rift. Frontline team leads and individual contributors required distinct narrative structures and design principles.

Recent findings suggest that having used e-learning platforms myself, I remember the frustration of opening a tool without a clear sense of my current standing, core strengths, or slipping metrics. That personal experience directly guided the individual contributor workspace; it needed to act as a highly tailored, self-directed mirror that was granular, honest, and personal.

Conversely, the manager’s interface had to bypass individual milestones initially to provide a macro pulse check on team vulnerabilities. It was designed around a different operational reality: how is the group progressing, and where are the consistent gaps? The view prioritised the aggregate picture first, while retaining an intuitive path to drill down into tactical day-to-day coordination when needed.

It has been revealed that our insight strategy was locked in during the early conceptual phase, long before wireframing a single chart. We intentionally abandoned the idea of building a dense, passive data log and focused on pacing the narrative arc.

For individual contributors, the core value was self-direction, ensuring they could glance at the interface on a Monday morning and immediately derive a clear priority list for the week ahead.

Sources indicate that for managers, the goal was to fundamentally shift the timing of operational conversations, providing them with the necessary baseline to intervene before a skill gap evolved into a critical project failure. The visualisations needed to surface the exact moments when a human check-in would be useful, shifting their workflow from reactive post-mortems to proactive guidance.

It has been revealed that the comparison tool was the highlight nobody had asked for. A manager dashboard and an individual dashboard are easy to anticipate. What is harder to land is: what if a manager wants to compare two specific team members against the same metrics, side by side? That view came from a design assumption, and it turned out to be the feature that resonated most.

The decisions that mattered most in this project weren’t in the initial brief — capturing data they hadn’t thought to request, and structuring it to answer questions they had not previously known how to articulate, which is the core differentiator of a user-centric data strategy.

In a recent development, the choice of visualisation layout must follow the geometric nature of the data itself. For this project, the core design problem was enabling an individual user to answer a specific question at a single glance: across eight distinct competency areas, where are my relative strengths and gaps?

Recent findings suggest that to solve this, we mapped the data using a radar chart. By organising multiple variables across axes radiating from a central point using polar coordinates, the interface connects the data points to form a single, unified shape. An even, balanced polygon instantly signals well-rounded proficiency, while a sharply skewed shape draws the eye immediately to an outlier area.

While a traditional linear bar chart would have forced the viewer to scan eight individual bars and mentally calculate the variance, a concentric, radial layout segments the data layers to make progress tracking and skill gaps immediately readable. When all dimensions share an identical scale and scoring method, the radar chart is not an unconventional aesthetic choice — it is the most functional tool for multi-dimensional analysis.

Industry observers note that the colour system was the other decision made early, and I mean early. During the branding exercise, each of the three products was assigned a colour. That colour did not stay in the brand guidelines. It was built into the data model from the beginning, running consistently across every chart, every filter, every breakdown. By the time a user landed on the dashboard for the first time, the mental model was already in place. They had not been taught the language. They already knew it.

Industry observers note that the shift from passive information to active insight revealed up first in how the dashboard was actually used. Following the deployment of the personalised dashboards and side-by-side team comparison tools, weekly active engagement on the platform’s analytics features rose noticeably, per internally reported figures. Managers were no longer opening the tool once a month to pull static reports. They were using it every Monday morning to actively plan their week.

Revenue and user growth also moved in the right direction over the following two quarters, though — as with most single-project outcomes — it’s hard to isolate the dashboard’s exact contribution from everything else that changed at the same time. The client reported churn across the platform falling to one of its lowest points on record. The clearest evidence of impact came from qualitative feedback. Managers reported that instead of using data to dissect a ‘bad’ month after the fact, the visualisations allowed them to instantly spot slipping performance and schedule a quick supportive catch-up before it turned into a real gap.

Data design reaches its full potential when visual presentation is treated as an upstream architectural choice rather than a downstream formatting step. Bringing structured UX thinking to data turns visualisations into active decision-making engines, ensuring every chart, report, and metric directly serves a human purpose:.

It has been revealed that the next time you are tasked with creating a data visualisation — whether it is an enterprise dashboard, an executive report, or a public-facing infographic — step away from the design canvas and BI tools. Focus your initial effort on the human decisions behind the screen. Only then will your data stop being a passive log of the past and start driving the direction of the future.

Mutabor Unveils the Voith brand identity

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (434 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.
  • The whole system starts with a single chevron.
  • The custom typeface carries the voice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

The whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking newly introduced ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

The custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it shows in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

Sources indicate that one frame indicates the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

Sources indicate that the system proves itself where the organization actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

Some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

Should I Quit My Job? A Decision Framework

📅 27 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1881 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • Sources indicate that feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit.
  • The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

The one number that changes everything.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

Sources indicate that feeling frustrated on a Monday morning is not a reason to quit. But persistent patterns that affect your health, relationships, and long-term career growth are legitimate signals worth examining. The challenge is separating temporary frustration from genuine misalignment.

The FI community approaches this differently from mainstream career advice. Instead of asking "Am I happy at work?" — which fluctuates daily — we ask: "Is this role aligned with my long-term financial and personal goals?" That reframe turns an emotional decision into a strategic one.

Before you submit your resignation, your finances need to be ready regardless of how miserable you are. Quitting without financial preparation trades one source of stress for another.

The FI community has a massive advantage here. If you have been building toward financial independence — even if you are not there yet — your savings provide a runway that most people do not have. A $200,000 investment portfolio at a 4% safe withdrawal rate provides $8,000 per year in sustainable income, which dramatically reduces the pressure of a job search.

The worst time to make a career decision is when you are emotionally overwhelmed. A terrible meeting, a passed-over promotion, or a toxic interaction with a coworker can make quitting feel urgent when the situation may actually be temporary or fixable.

Sources indicate that use the 30-day test: if you have wanted to quit for fewer than 30 consecutive days, it is likely a temporary frustration. If the feeling has persisted — or intensified — for 30+ days, it is a pattern worth taking seriously.

In a recent development, how you leave a job matters as much as why you leave. Your professional reputation follows you for your entire career, and the people you work with today may be the hiring managers, clients, or references of tomorrow.

Industry observers note that two weeks notice: This is the minimum professional standard in the United States. For senior roles, three to four weeks is more appropriate. Check your employment contract — some roles require 30, 60, or 90 days notice.

Sources indicate that the resignation conversation: Schedule a private meeting with your direct manager. Keep it brief and positive. Say: "I have decided to move on to a new opportunity. I want to thank you for [specific positive thing], and I am committed to making the transition as smooth as possible. My last day would be [date].".

It has been revealed that the transition plan: Document your ongoing projects, key contacts, passwords, and processes. Offer to train your replacement. Complete as much outstanding work as possible. A strong exit creates goodwill that pays dividends for years.

What not to do: Do not badmouth the organization, your boss, or your coworkers — not in the resignation meeting, not in your exit interview, not on social media. Even if your grievances are legitimate, airing them publicly hurts your reputation more than theirs.

Conventional advice claims never quit without another job lined up. The FI community takes a more nuanced view: it depends on your financial position and the severity of the situation.

Recent findings suggest that if you are leaving due to company changes — layoffs, restructuring, or role elimination — negotiate your severance package. Many employees accept the first offer without realizing severance is negotiable. Key leverage points include your tenure, difficulty of replacement, willingness to sign a non-compete or non-disparagement clause, and any outstanding commissions or bonuses.

Common severance components to negotiate: extended pay (push for 2-4 weeks per year of tenure), continued health insurance coverage, outplacement services, vesting acceleration for equity, and a positive reference commitment.

According to recent reports, health insurance is often the biggest financial concern when leaving a job. You have two primary options:.

COBRA: Continues your employer initiative for up to 18 months. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer was paying) plus a 2% administrative fee. COBRA typically costs $500-$700 per month for individual coverage and $1,400-$2,000+ for family coverage. It is expensive but familiar.

It has been revealed that ACA Marketplace: Depending on your income after leaving, you may qualify for substantial subsidies. If your annual income drops below 400% of the federal poverty level, premium tax credits can reduce your monthly cost to $100-$400 for comprehensive coverage. FI seekers who leave jobs often qualify for significant subsidies because their earned income drops even if their net worth is high — ACA subsidies are based on income, not wealth.

Here is where financial independence changes everything. When you have significant savings — even if you have not reached full FI — you have leverage that most employees lack. You can negotiate from strength, take career risks, and walk away from toxic situations without financial desperation.

Recent findings suggest that A $500,000 portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate provides $20,000 per year indefinitely. That is not enough to live on for most people, but combined with a working spouse, reduced expenses, or part-time work, it transforms "should I quit my job" from a terrifying question into a strategic calculation. FI is not just about never working again — it is about having the financial security to make career decisions based on alignment and purpose rather than desperation and fear.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The FI community has a saying: financial independence is not about quitting your job — it is about having the freedom to choose whether to keep it. Every dollar you save and invest is a vote for your future autonomy. When you have 12-24 months of expenses saved, you negotiate from strength. When you reach Coast FI or beyond, a bad job becomes a choice, not a trap. Build your FI runway and the question changes from "Can I afford to quit?" to "Does this role still serve my goals?".

Work through these steps before making your decision.

Have you consistently wanted to leave for 30+ days? If no, wait. Temporary frustration is not a reason to upend your career. If yes, proceed to step two.

It has been revealed that pro tip: Keep a brief daily journal noting your satisfaction level 1-10. Data beats feelings for decision-making.

Is the glitch your boss, your role, your compensation, the culture, or the industry? Some problems follow you to the next job. A bad manager is fixable by transferring. An industry you hate requires a bigger change.

Verify your emergency fund, health insurance options, debt situation, and FI runway. If you are not financially ready, keep working while you build your safety net and search for alternatives.

It has been revealed that before quitting, have you requested a transfer, a raise, a role change, or a conversation with HR? Many solvable problems go unaddressed because employees assume the answer will be no.

Pro tip: A direct conversation with your manager about your concerns resolves the issue 40% of the time.

If you decide to leave, secure your next opportunity (if possible), give appropriate notice, document your work for your successor, and maintain every professional relationship.

According to recent reports, pro tip: Never burn bridges. The colleague you leave today may be the hiring manager at your dream firm in three years.

Sources indicate that at minimum, 3-6 months of essential expenses in a liquid savings account. If you are quitting without another job lined up, aim for 6-12 months. The FI community recommends having your emergency fund fully funded, health insurance secured, and ideally some progress toward financial independence to provide a psychological safety net.

If your job is causing persistent anxiety, depression, or physical health symptoms that do not improve with coping strategies, therapy, or workplace changes — yes, your health must come first. But do it strategically: secure health insurance, build your financial runway, and consult a therapist or career coach before making the leap. Never make a permanent career decision during a temporary emotional crisis.

Industry observers note that generally, quitting gives you more control over the narrative, timing, and terms. Being fired can qualify you for unemployment benefits (quitting usually does not), but it can also create a negative reference. If you sense a termination is coming, consider whether negotiating a mutual separation with severance is an option. Document everything and consult an employment attorney if you believe the termination may be discriminatory or retaliatory.

Industry observers note that be honest and frame it positively. Acceptable explanations include: career transition (took time to retrain or earn a certification), personal development (traveled, volunteered, or cared for family), or strategic job search (took time to find the right fit rather than settling). Employers increasingly accept career gaps — especially post-2020 — as long as you can articulate what you did during the time off.

In a recent development, COBRA (Consolidated Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act) lets you continue your employer health plan for up to 18 months after leaving. You pay the full premium (your share plus what your employer contributed) plus a 2% admin fee. Individual coverage typically costs $500-$700/month and family coverage runs $1,400-$2,000+/month. The ACA marketplace is often cheaper, especially if your income drops after leaving.

FI savings transform the equation entirely. With a substantial portfolio, you have a financial runway that removes the urgency and desperation from the decision. Even partial FI — having 2-5 years of expenses invested — means you can quit a toxic job, take time to find the right next role, or transition to lower-paying but more fulfilling work. FI is not just about retiring early; it is about having the leverage to make career decisions from a position of strength rather than fear.

The question "should I quit my job?" deserves a framework, not an impulse. Apply the 30-day test, diagnose the real problem, verify your financial readiness, explore internal solutions, and then make a deliberate decision. If you have been building toward financial independence, your savings give you something most people lack: the freedom to walk away from a bad situation without financial panic. FI is the ultimate career insurance — it turns "I have to stay" into "I choose to stay or go." Build your runway, protect your reputation, and make the decision from a position of strength.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the objects we carry often reveal more about us than we realize. From the jewelry we wear to the accessories we keep within reach, even the smallest possessions become expressions of personal style. Yet as technology plays an increasingly central role in our lives, the devices we interact with most remain largely defined by their utility. Bringing more personality to these everyday essentials is the idea behind Pocket Full of Joy—a latest collaboration between ESR, a consumer tech accessories brand, and creative duo Craig & Karl—which transforms phone cases and wallets into colorful, functional accessories.

Known for their vibrant compositions and playful iconography, Craig & Karl bring their distinctive visual language to a collection of iPhone cases and magnetic wallets. The collaboration draws upon the duo’s affinity for bold colors and familiar imagery, translating their graphic sensibilities into objects designed to accompany their owners throughout the day. The result is a collection that explores how artistic expression can become part of everyday life.

It has been revealed that across the collection, sticker-like illustrations, saturated hues, and expressive typography lend a sense of character to otherwise utilitarian surfaces. A collage of playful symbols evokes the spontaneity of a personal scrapbook, while the graphic “OK” design introduces a lighthearted note of optimism. Elsewhere, the cheerful “HI” motif transforms a magnetic wallet into a small, portable greeting. Each composition reflects Craig & Karl’s recognizable aesthetic while giving everyday accessories a more personal character.

According to recent reports, behind the playful graphics are the practical features that define ESR’s accessories. The Classic Hybrid Magnetic Case with Flex Stand incorporates a built-in adjustable stand, MagSafe compatibility, and protective construction, allowing it to move between different activities without sacrificing its colorful design. Coordinating magnetic wallets hold cards and cash in compact silhouettes, while the Magnetic Wallet Stand with Grip adds an adjustable viewing stand and finger loop for greater versatility. Together, these features bring Craig & Karl’s expressive graphics to everyday accessories.

The collection’s appeal also comes from the way it brings art into objects that have become nearly inseparable from modern life. Where traditional artworks invite observation, these designs encourage interaction, becoming more personal through repeated use. A phone placed on a café table, a wallet retrieved during a morning commute, or a device propped against a desk becomes a small, unexpected moment of visual interest.

Recent findings suggest that with Pocket Full of Joy, ESR and Craig & Karl make a case for bringing more creativity into the everyday. Sometimes, the most memorable design details are found in the things we carry without a second thought.

The ESR × Craig & Karl Pocket Full of Joy collection will be available Nov. 14, 2026, at esr.com and amazon.com, with iPhone cases starting at $49.99 and magnetic wallets starting at $25.99.

For a new residence in Orange County, California, interior designer Lindye Galloway approached that challenge through a careful balance of natural materials, layered textures, and sculptural furnishings. The goal was to create a home that felt as warm and comfortable as it was refined, with a relaxed atmosphere suited to everyday family life.

According to recent reports, galloway drew inspiration from the architecture and natural surroundings, aiming to create a timeless home. The interiors are organized around texture and natural materials in a soft, understated palette. Warm woods, soft neutrals, and natural stone run through the rooms alongside linen, wool, and mohair.

Tactile upholstery and darker accents contrast with the lighter woods and stone, adding depth and dimension to each room. Furniture was selected for comfort and sculptural appeal, with clean lines and soft, organic forms, giving rooms a relaxed, lived-in quality.

The attention to detail extends to the home’s fixtures and finishes. Hardware from Rocky Mountain Hardware and Nanz is complemented by mirrors from Claude Home and Croft House, while lighting comes from Ravenhill, Atelier de Troupe, and Roll & Hill.

In a recent development, the kitchen, primary bathroom, and living room carry the same combination of wood, stone, and natural fibers. Beyond the main rooms, the property includes a separate guest house with its own bedroom and an indoor-outdoor living area. Galloway extended the same material palette to these spaces, creating continuity throughout the property.

In a recent development, rather than relying on dramatic gestures, Galloway lets the interplay of materials, textures, and forms define the interiors. It’s an approach that brings warmth and intimacy to a home of considerable scale.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

Industry observers note that that contract is officially changing. Driven by advances in artificial intelligence and large language models, a upcoming generation of web tools is pioneering a radical philosophy: Intent-Driven Design. Rather than expecting our consumers to learn complex menus and click through elaborate sales funnels, these platforms operate by capturing high-level human goals and silently executing the grunt work in the background.

This vision builds on long-standing HCI concepts like Golden Krishna’s “The Best Interface Is No Interface” and Don Norman’s principles of human-centered design.

The ultimate goal of modern web design is no longer to build prettier buttons or flashy animations; it is to eliminate the interface entirely.

Well, at least what we understand based on our current experience.

It is essential for UX designers to understand the changes we’re witnessing and even re-evaluate our role, shifting our focus from designing visible interfaces to guiding transparent, intent-driven AI experiences.

To understand where web design is going, we first have to look at the friction we have accepted as “normal” for decades.

Consider the traditional workflow of buying a flight online. The user experience is intentionally hyper-interactive:.

Sources indicate that this is a classic point-and-click UI paradigm. The computer acts as a passive container of data, and the human acts as the orchestrator, manually inputting parameters, interpreting raw outputs, and executing each micro-step along the way.

Sources indicate that intent-driven design flips this dynamic entirely. Instead of forcing you to navigate the mechanical steps of how to find a flight, the interface asks a simple question: What are you trying to accomplish?

When you express a goal, such as “Find me a non-stop flight to Chicago next weekend under $300 that arrives before 5 PM”, the software reads your intent, executes the multi-step search query behind the scenes, compares the options, and presents a single actionable resolution. The ten clicks dissolve into one clear intent outcome.

This shift isn’t a theoretical vision of the distant future. Some of the world’s most accessible websites allow you to experience intent-capturing systems already.

Traditional search engines like Google were built as directories. You typed a keyword, and the interface rewarded you with ten blue links. The actual work of opening five tabs, skimming long articles, dodging ads, and manually assembling an answer was left to you. Although this is now changing, with AI content appearing first when you search on Google.

Industry observers note that perplexity AI allows anyone to perform instant intent-based searches. Instead of forcing you to click into multiple tabs, the interface synthesises the perfect result for your context.

Recent findings suggest that for years, creating a website meant using visual builders like Figma or drag-and-drop web editors. As designers, we spent hours manually drawing rectangles, picking hexadecimal colour codes, adjusting padding values, and sometimes writing CSS code.

Vercel v0 lets anyone test its generative interface builder right from the home page without signing in.

Many traditional productivity tools require you to manually construct task lists, drag items across Kanban boards, and assign micro-deadlines. Goblin.tools is a free, single-page suite of single-task AI tools designed specifically for neurodivergent users or anyone feeling overwhelmed, requiring zero sign-ups or configuration.

When you remove traditional menus, sidebars, and forms, how do you keep a website usable? Designers pioneering this space rely on three core pillars:.

It has been revealed that an invisible interface doesn’t always wait for you to type a command — it leverages context to anticipate user needs. Guided by industry standards like Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines on Contextual & Ambient Design, modern systems read environmental metadata, such as device state, location, and past interaction patterns, to trigger proactive actions.

In traditional web design, every user sees the exact same layout. An e-commerce store shows the same navigation bar whether you are a first-time visitor looking for customer support or a returning customer tracking a package.

As highlighted in the Nielsen Norman Group’s analysis on AI as a upcoming UX paradigm, computing is shifting from command-based interaction to outcome-specification. This enables Generative UI, where interfaces are rendered dynamically on the fly based on what you are trying to do in that exact moment. For example, platforms like Vercel v0 demonstrate how raw intent can instantly render functional code components without manual layout building. If you express a desire to compute complex financial data, the interface generates a dynamic calculator widget on demand, receding once your goal is completed.

Traditional interfaces are obsessed with prevention, constantly peppering users with confirmation pop-ups (“Are you sure you want to delete this file?”).

According to recent reports, intent-driven interfaces adapt Jakob Nielsen’s 10 Usability Heuristics on User Control and Error Recovery by shifting the safety net from prevention to easy reversibility. Because autonomous agents take actions on your behalf, products prioritise frictionless rollback mechanisms. A prominent “Undo” button, simple revision prompts (“Make this summary shorter”), and transparent audit logs replace intrusive warning modals.

While removing interface friction is liberating, stripping away visual controls introduces significant product design challenges. When software acts on inferred intent rather than direct point-and-click commands, designers must navigate critical ethical and technical pitfalls.

It has been revealed that when a website makes decisions for you, it can swiftly feel patronising or invasive. As explored by the Stanford Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) Group, automation must maintain clear boundaries to prevent user frustration. Furthermore, ethical frameworks from the Center for Humane Technology emphasise that product designers must guard against manipulative defaults.

Designers must strike a delicate balance: automate routine execution, but explicitly prompt the user for high-stakes confirmations (such as financial transactions, publishing public content, or altering privacy settings).

In a traditional UI, if you get an unexpected result, you can usually diagnose the problem — perhaps you checked the wrong filter box or selected an incorrect date.

In a recent development, with an intent-driven interface, troubleshooting becomes harder. To address this “black box” challenge, the Google PAIR (People + AI Research) Guidebook advocates for transparent feedback loops. The system must explicitly state its interpretation (“Searching for non-stop flights to Chicago under $300…”) so users can calibrate trust and correct misinterpretations instantly.

As a UX designer, always being curious to understand how our design approach is changing in the world of AI, I find it essential that we re-evaluate the foundational elements of our craft.

Rather than designing static buttons and rigid forms, we need to learn to map and present dynamic, generative UI components that adapt on the fly to user intent.

By mastering these evolving patterns, like ambient feedback, inline prompts, and transparent AI status indicators, we can ensure that screenless, agent-driven tools remain intuitive, ethical, and deeply human-centered.

According to recent reports, for decades, the digital industry has evaluated software success through engagement metrics like time spent in app, click-through rates, and page views per session. Websites were deliberately engineered to maximise visual engagement and interaction volume.

The philosophy behind Golden Krishna’s seminal book The Best Interface Is No Interface, aligned with the broader Center for Humane Technology’s Time Well Spent movement, turns these metrics on their head. The ultimate test of a modern digital product is no longer how visually captivating its buttons are, but rather: How effectively did this software solve the problem and get out of the user’s way?,.

It has been revealed that we are entering an era where web applications will no longer be measured by the beauty of their interfaces, but by their ability to render those complex interfaces completely obsolete. The future of the web isn’t more interaction — it is seamless, invisible completion.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, technology has become so thoroughly integrated into our lives that it’s easy to overlook the design behind it. But look beyond the specifications, and you’ll find plenty of objects worth paying attention to: a clock that uses light and sound to mark the passing hours, a digital frame that resembles a printed photograph, and a cassette-playing boombox that brings back the pleasure of physical controls.

Industry observers note that for this year’s tech gift guide, we’ve selected 18 products that put as much thought into how they look and feel as what they do. Some embrace the past, others experiment with newly introduced technology, and a few make the everyday business of charging, organizing, and staying connected a little more enjoyable.

Photography courtesy of MoMA Design Store.

The boombox is back, complete with oversized speakers, analog controls, and illuminated VU meters. Studebaker’s retro-inspired design brings the 1980s into the present with Bluetooth connectivity, a CD player, USB playback, and a cassette deck that can even record music. A rechargeable battery and built-in carrying handle make it easy to take the nostalgia wherever the party goes.

The SB214OS Bluetooth Boombox is available at store.moma.org for $250.

Photography courtesy of Polaroid.

Sources indicate that polaroid’s Mod puts creative controls directly on the camera, inviting experimentation without the distraction of a smartphone screen. Dedicated physical controls make it easy to explore effects like double exposures, light painting, motion freeze, and split-shot compositions. It’s a refreshingly hands-on approach to photography that encourages a little spontaneity and plenty of happy accidents.

The Polaroid Mod Instant Camera is available at polaroid.com for $169.99.

Photography courtesy of Therabody.

Sources indicate that therabody takes a different approach to workout recovery with a device designed to fit between your hands. To help manage body heat during workouts, the handheld device uses temperature-controlled surfaces to cool both palms simultaneously, with additional heat and contrast therapy settings. Compact and cordless, it provides an alternative to ice baths and other more cumbersome temperature-based recovery equipment.

The CryoTherm Palm is available at therabody.com for $399.99.

Photography courtesy of Balmuda.

Sources indicate that inspired by traditional pocket watches, Balmuda’s The Clock reimagines how we experience time through light, sound, and movement. Its carved aluminum body houses 75 LEDs that create an animated display, while built-in speakers play ambient soundscapes designed for focus, relaxation, and sleep. With customizable alarms, app connectivity, and USB-C charging, it’s a thoughtful alternative to the conventional bedside clock.

The Clock is available at us.balmuda.com for $499 in Silver and $519 in Champagne.

Photography courtesy of Bang & Olufsen.

Sources indicate that bang & Olufsen’s Beoplay H100 headphones are undeniably a splurge, but they’re designed with longevity in mind. The Danish brand developed the H100 with replaceable components, including the ear cushions, headband, and batteries. The custom titanium drivers, soft leather detailing, and rich color options give them a distinctly luxurious feel, while advanced noise cancellation and immersive sound make the listening experience just as considered as the design. It’s an investment piece for someone who appreciates exceptional craftsmanship as much as great audio.

The Beoplay H100 Headphones are available at bang-olufsen.com for $2,200.

Photography courtesy of Warby Parker.

It has been revealed that smart glasses are getting a stylish update thanks to Warby Parker’s collaboration with Google and Samsung. Available in three of the brand’s familiar silhouettes, the lightweight frames incorporate a camera, open-ear speakers, and Gemini AI for hands-free photography, calls, navigation, and more. Subtly translucent temples offer a glimpse of the technology inside without compromising the classic eyewear design. With prescription, nonprescription, reading, and sunglass options, they’re a surprisingly versatile gift.

Intelligent Eyewear is available for preorder at warbyparker.com, starting at $395.

Photography courtesy of Flowtica.

What looks like an ordinary ballpoint pen has a few technological tricks up its sleeve. The Flowtica Scribe combines a functional writing instrument with an AI-powered voice recorder, allowing consumers to capture conversations while taking notes on paper the old-fashioned way. A companion app can transcribe recordings and turn them into summaries and action items, bringing digital convenience to a familiar analog tool. An optional vegan leather charging case gives the device a place to rest between meetings.

The Flowtica Scribe is available at flowtica.ai for $159.

Photography courtesy of Bellroy.

Anyone who’s ever untangled a mess of charging cables at the bottom of a bag will appreciate Bellroy’s thoughtfully designed Tech Kit. The small organizer opens flat to reveal a series of mesh pockets and elastic loops that keep chargers, cables, earbuds, and other tech essentials neatly in place. Its structured shape makes everything easy to see and access, while the streamlined exterior, made from recycled woven fabric, slips neatly into a backpack or carry-on. It’s a simple solution to one of travel’s most persistent little annoyances.

The Tech Kit is available at bellroy.com for $59–$69, depending on color.

Amazon’s latest Kindle redesign brings a more refined look and feel to the familiar e-reader. The Paperwhite Signature Edition pairs a sleek aluminum body with a 7-inch, glare-free display, adjustable warm lighting, and double-tap page turning. Waterproof construction and wireless charging make it an easy travel companion, while two finishes, Graphite and Seaglass Green, offer a choice between classic and colorful.

The Kindle Paperwhite Signature Edition is available at amazon.com for $250.

Photography courtesy of Daily Objects.

It has been revealed that who notes charging stations have to be boring? DailyObjects’ Surge Foldaway turns an everyday tech essential into a sculptural desktop accessory. Its adjustable design accommodates an iPhone, Apple Watch, and AirPods simultaneously, consolidating three charging spots into one tidy footprint. The bold Cosmic Orange finish adds a welcome pop of color, giving the accessory a presence even when the devices are elsewhere.

The Surge Foldaway 3-in-1 Wireless Charger is available at dailyobjects.us for $175.

Photography courtesy of ModRetro.

A love letter to handheld gaming, ModRetro’s Chromatic brings the original Game Boy experience into the present with a few thoughtful upgrades. Its magnesium-alloy body houses a custom, pixel-perfect display designed to play original Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges. The colorful finishes include four translucent options that expose the internal hardware, turning the console’s components into part of its visual identity.

The Chromatic + Tetris Bundle is available at modretro.com starting at $199.

Industry observers note that shark’s CryoGlow Plus combines two skincare technologies in a single wearable device: LED light therapy and under-eye cooling. Red, blue, and infrared lights power several treatment modes, while adjustable cooling pads help refresh tired eyes. The upgraded design offers improved LED coverage around the eyes and mouth, and the soft Pastel Berry finish makes this wearable gadget surprisingly stylish.

The CryoGlow Plus LED Face Mask is available at sharkninja.com for $379.99.

In a market crowded with phones competing for attention, the Mudita Kompakt is designed to demand less of it. Its minimalist design centers on a 4.3-inch E Ink display, favoring a restrained interface over colorful notifications and app-heavy screens. Essential features like calling, messaging, offline maps, and a camera remain, while a dedicated offline switch offers a physical way to disconnect.

The Mudita Kompakt is available at mudita.com for $399.

Sources indicate that who claims smart technology has to look high-tech? Birdfy’s Feeder Wood combines the charm of a traditional wooden birdhouse with a built-in camera, letting bird lovers watch their feathered visitors up close. Made from FSC-certified wood, the solar-powered feeder captures 1080p video. Its companion app can identify more than 6,000 bird species, bringing a layer of digital discovery to an otherwise familiar backyard ritual.

The Feeder Wood is available at birdfy.com for $189.99.

According to recent reports, wallie’s approach to the digital photo frame starts with a simple idea: make the screen look less like a screen. Its 10-inch color E Ink display gives photographs the appearance of printed images, while real wood construction and a choice of four finishes help it blend into a gallery wall or shelf arrangement. Rounded or square corners offer further customization, and a rechargeable battery eliminates the need for a visible power cord. Photos can be updated remotely through an app.

The Wallie 10 is available at shop.wallieframe.com for $299.

According to recent reports, with its simple spherical form, Eve Flare looks more like an illuminated object than a conventional lamp. The rechargeable, water-resistant light offers millions of customizable colors, with app and voice controls for setting the mood indoors or outside. Its wireless charging base and portable design mean it can move effortlessly from a bedside table to the patio, adding a little atmosphere wherever it lands.

The Eve Flare Portable Smart LED Lamp is available at apple.com for $99.95.

Photography courtesy of Best Buy.

Sources indicate that 8BitDo borrows the visual language of the original Nintendo Entertainment System for a mechanical keyboard that feels straight out of the 1980s. Chunky gray keys, red accents, and tactile mechanical switches establish the retro aesthetic, while an included joystick and two oversized programmable buttons bring arcade-style controls to the desktop. Bluetooth and wireless connectivity keep the throwback design compatible with contemporary setups.

The 8BitDo Retro Mechanical Keyboard N Edition is available at bestbuy.com for $79.99.

Photography courtesy of Orbitkey.

Even the most organized desk tends to accumulate charging cables, adapters, and other small tech accessories. Orbitkey’s Nest v2 gives them a designated home in a compact storage box with adjustable dividers and a fabric-lined interior. The removable leather-covered lid doubles as a valet tray and 15W wireless charger, keeping everyday essentials within reach while concealing the clutter underneath.

The Nest v2 is available at orbitkey.com for $125.

Nan Goldin to debut new film exploring nature and extinction in first UK solo museum show in over two decades

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise.
  • According to recent reports, what links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation?
  • Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for audiences who associate the US photographer Nan Goldin with the friends and lovers of her slideshow The Ballad of Sexual Dependency (1973-86), her forthcoming Hayward Gallery exhibition may come as a surprise. Animals, a solar eclipse and footage salvaged from nature documentaries will feature in Goldin’s first institutional solo show in the UK since her 2002 retrospective at the Whitechapel Gallery.

According to recent reports, what links these subjects to the photographs that established her reputation? According to the Hayward’s chief curator, Rachel Thomas, the connection lies in the relationships Goldin creates through the camera, rather than the identities of those who appear before it. In Thomas’s reading, Goldin’s focus on queer communities and chosen family has widened to embrace the natural world.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part II, 2026.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

Rather than being a retrospective, the exhibition You Never Did Anything Wrong presents new and recent work by Goldin. Thomas, who worked with the photographer at the Irish Museum of Modern Art in 2017, tells The Art Newspaper: “I wanted to collaborate again to reveal where her practice is moving now.” Four years in the making, the exhibition is the Hayward’s contribution to the Southbank Centre’s 75th-anniversary programme devoted to “visionaries who have fundamentally redefined culture”.

The show’s centrepiece will be the premiere of You never did anything wrong, Part II (2026). Created with the film-maker David Sherman, it draws on 16mm nature documentaries from the 1960s and 70s, and damaged soundtracks from old films, with a fresh score by the British musician Mica Levi. Goldin turns material associated with explaining the natural world into an abstract meditation on animals, land and impending extinction.

Nan Goldin, Still from You never did anything wrong, Part I, 2024.

© Nan Goldin, courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

It accompanies You never did anything wrong, Part I (2024), which centres on a solar eclipse and draws on a myth of animals stealing the sun. Together, the films bring Goldin’s work into a world without human protagonists.

Industry observers note that elsewhere, Stendhal Syndrome (2024), receiving its UK premiere, places photographs of her friends and lovers in dialogue with classical art, accompanied by a score by Soundwalk Collective. Memory Lost (2019-21), meanwhile, returns to addiction, connecting personal experience to Goldin’s campaigning with Pain (Prescription Addiction Intervention Now), the group she founded to confront the opioid crisis in the US.

Art of intimacy: Young Love (2024) is one of Goldin’s works in Stendhal Syndrome © Nan Goldin; courtesy the artist and Gagosian.

For Thomas, compassion connects these changing subjects. Goldin’s importance lies partly in her refusal to maintain a distance from the people she photographs, with the exhibition proposing that this approach can extend beyond her own community. “What endures across every medium and chapter is an exploration of compassion,” Thomas says. “Goldin simply expands the horizon of who and what is embraced by her gaze.”.

• You Never Did Anything Wrong, Hayward Gallery, London, 24 November-14 March 2027.

#103167. OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (683 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Design-milk ↗ Open Full Page

OMA Rethinks Retail Through Craft and Circular Design at Potato Head Bali

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (683 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Design-milk

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made?
  • Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.
  • “Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

What if a store invited visitors to consider not just what they’re buying, but how it’s made? At Desa Potato Head in Bali, the newly introduced Good Times General Store explores that question through architecture, craftsmanship, and circular design. Created in collaboration with OMA, Potato Head’s first permanent retail space shifts the focus from consumption to discovery, inviting visitors to engage with the materials and processes behind the products.

Building on a partnership spanning more than a decade, OMA and Potato Head envisioned the store as an extension of the hospitality brand’s “Good Times, Do Good” philosophy.

“Rather than focusing solely on the display and sale of products, the design prioritizes experience, participation and interaction,” explains David Gianotten, OMA managing partner and architect.

Recent findings suggest that the architecture embraces a “contemporary-traditional” approach, bringing Balinese vernacular building techniques into a modern setting. An alang-alang thatch façade, made from locally sourced tropical grass, creates a textured outer layer, while rammed-earth walls made from local clay lend the interior a grounded, tactile quality. Bamboo appears throughout, including in the terrazzo flooring, where it’s used as an aggregate, and in the display elements.

“We wanted to reinterpret Balinese traditional architecture and craftsmanship in a contemporary way, rather than simply reproducing traditional forms or decorative elements,” says Ade Herkarisma, group head of architecture and development at Potato Head.

Sources indicate that reclaimed and locally sourced materials bring natural variations in color, texture, and form. Instead of concealing these irregularities, the designers embraced them, letting the materials guide the assembly and detailing.

Inside, the store unfolds across five interconnected bays, guiding visitors from finished products toward the processes behind their creation. The first showcases souvenirs and lifestyle objects by Indonesian craftspeople, while the second presents the Potato Head Collection, an apparel line inspired by Bali. The third introduces Wasted by Potato Head, a collaboration with British designer Max Lamb that transforms discarded materials into furniture and homewares.

It has been revealed that in the final two bays, visitors move from browsing to making. A working natural dye studio transforms food and plant waste into pigments used in workshops exploring dyeing, painting, and pattern-making. Beyond it, The Workshop features a wall of shredded HDPE plastic recovered from waste collectors across Bali and Java. The colorful fragments become part of the architecture, making the material’s previous life visible, while the surrounding space is dedicated to experimentation.

“While the first three bays focus on products and the stories behind them, the final two bays prioritize participation, inviting visitors to engage directly with materials and processes,” Gianotten explains.

It has been revealed that the store also connects to Desa Potato Head’s broader sustainability initiatives, including its Waste Lab and Follow the Waste Tour, which demonstrate how discarded materials can be recovered, processed, and transformed into new objects. For OMA, the project extends ideas explored in N*thing is Possible, a 2022 exhibition in Singapore examining the potential of zero-waste hospitality.

“Circularity therefore becomes something experiential rather than abstract,” says Gianotten.

Designing around reclaimed resources required flexibility, especially around material consistency and availability. Rather than forcing materials into predetermined specifications, the team adapted the design to their natural characteristics and limitations.

“We discovered that circularity goes beyond material selection,” Herkarisma explains. “It is about rethinking how we design, build, operate, and engage people in the process of giving upcoming value to resources that would otherwise be discarded.”.

At the Good Times General Store, the act of making is as visible as the finished product. By placing workshops alongside retail displays and allowing reclaimed materials to shape the architecture, OMA and Potato Head offer a model of shopping that encourages visitors to look more closely at what they consume—and what might otherwise be thrown away.

Sources indicate that murrye Bernard is an architect-turned-writer covering architecture, interiors, product design, and sustainability. A registered architect, she has written for Architect, Architectural Record, Metropolis, Hospitality Design, Texas Architect, Green Building Advisor, and The Architect's Newspaper. She previously served as managing editor of Contract magazine and enjoys exploring the intersection of design, materials, and culture.
